sections.name: MCQ Set A
tips: Read the attribution line first: who wrote it, when, and why. A Ming official, a Muslim scholar and a modern historian each have a different purpose.
Find the main idea of each paragraph before you look at the choices. Many questions ask about one paragraph only.

For "best used as evidence of" or "best illustrates" questions, first name the bigger development the source shows (more trade, Mongol connections, spread of religion, crops and disease), then pick the choice that matches it.
The wrong choices are usually true-but-not-in-the-source, from the wrong network or region, or too extreme. Cross them out with the X button.
"Practice passage" sources were written for this kit from your class materials. Only words inside quotation marks that are labeled as real are real quotations, so don't quote the rest on the test.

A1.title: A king from beyond the desert, 1324
A1.attr: Practice passage in the voice of a Cairo official writing about a decade after Mansa Musa's visit.
A1.label: Practice passage written from your class materials (textbook, review sheet, slides); not a real quotation.
paras: In the year of the pilgrimage the king of Mali, Musa, came to Cairo on his way to Mecca with a retinue larger than any the city had seen. He and his companions spent and gave away so much gold to officials, merchants and the poor that its price in our markets fell sharply. Even now, twelve years later, the dealers in gold have not recovered their losses.

The king told us that his kingdom lay many months' journey to the south, beyond the great desert, and that its wealth came from the gold of his lands, which the caravans carry north to trade for the salt of the desert. He takes a share of all this trade, and his soldiers keep the roads open for the merchants.
He is a Muslim who prays as we do, and he said that he meant to return home with learned men and books, so that the scholars of his own cities might teach the law and the faith.

A2.title: Destroyers and connectors
A2.attr: Practice passage written in the style of a modern historian of the Mongol Empire.
A2.label: Practice passage written from your class materials (textbook, review sheet, slides); not a real quotation.
paras: The Mongols are remembered for slaughter, and the memory is deserved. Their armies used terror as a weapon, and when Hulegu took Baghdad in 1258, the city was sacked and the caliph killed. Cities that resisted were often destroyed so that others would surrender without a fight.

Yet the same conquerors made the long overland routes safer than they had been in centuries. Wherever Mongol authority reached, roads were repaired and bandits were punished, and the yam, a relay system of messengers and stations, linked distant provinces. Merchants who had once paid tolls to a dozen rival rulers now dealt with a single authority that respected trade, and the khans tolerated many religions, so traders of every faith were welcome.

It is no accident that the travelers who carried Greek and Islamic medicine, Hindu-Arabic numerals and Chinese technology between Asia and Europe moved in these decades. The Pax Mongolica was built on conquest, but it connected Afro-Eurasia as never before.

A3.title: A Persian envoy in Calicut, 1442
A3.attr: Practice passage built around the words of Abdu Razzak, a Persian envoy who visited Calicut in 1442. Only the sentence in quotation marks is his; it is quoted in your textbook.
A3.label: Practice passage written from your class materials; the quoted sentence is a real quotation from your textbook.
paras: Calicut, on the southwest coast of India, is known to merchants as the City of Spices. Ships come to it from the ports of Arabia and Persia when the winds of the monsoon carry them east, and junks from China also anchor in its harbor. Pepper, cotton cloth and the steel of India are loaded here for the return voyage.

The ruler of the city welcomes foreign merchants of every faith, and many Arab merchants have settled here, married and raised families. The envoy was struck most by how safe trade felt: "Wealthy merchants bring in big cargoes, which they unload and unhesitatingly send into the markets without thinking in the meantime of any security, or checking the account, or keeping watch over the goods."
Officers of the port collect the duties owed on the goods, and the ruler grows rich from this trade without sending out a single ship of his own.

A4.label: Adapted from a table in your textbook (AMSCO).

A5.title: After the great dying
A5.attr: Practice passage written in the style of a modern historian of medieval Europe.
A5.label: Practice passage written from your class materials (textbook, review sheet, slides); not a real quotation.
paras: The plague that reached Europe in 1347 traveled the same roads and sea lanes that had carried silk and spices. Fleas on rats rode in the holds of ships and among the bales of caravans, and the Mongol conquests that had joined Asia together helped carry the disease west. Between 1347 and 1351 it killed about a third of Europe's people, and many millions more in Asia.

The survivors inherited a changed world. In the countryside, so many workers had died that landowners who had once dictated terms to their tenants now competed for laborers. Wages rose, and peasants who could leave for better pay did so. The obligations that had tied workers to the land under feudalism began to weaken.

Trade and city life suffered in the short term, as markets emptied and cities lost many of their people. Writers such as Boccaccio, who lived through the plague in Florence, left accounts of the horror that historians still use today.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a claim made in the first paragraph?
options: Musa was robbed of most of his gold by the officials of Cairo during his stay
Musa's spending lowered the price of gold in Cairo for years
Musa's visit made Cairo's gold dealers rich for many years afterward
Musa came to Cairo to conquer it before going on to Mecca
questions.exp: So much gold flooded the market that its price fell, and dealers had not recovered twelve years later.
why: The paragraph says he spent and gave gold away.
The dealers had not recovered their losses.

questions.stem: The second paragraph can best be used as evidence that Mali's wealth came mainly from
options: selling Chinese porcelain and silk to merchants arriving by sea from India
conquering the cities of North Africa
salt mines in the heart of the kingdom
taxing and protecting the trans-Saharan gold trade
questions.exp: Gold went north for salt; the king took a share and his soldiers kept the roads open.
why: Mali is inland; its trade crossed the desert.
The paragraph describes trade, not conquest.
Salt came from the desert to the north.

questions.stem: Musa's plan in the third paragraph most directly contributed to which development?
options: The conversion of all West Africans to Islam within a single generation
Timbuktu's growth as a center of Islamic learning
The end of the trans-Saharan trade
Mali's conquest by Songhai

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the historian's main argument?
options: The Mongols were peaceful traders whose reputation for violence is unfair
The Mongols destroyed trade by sacking cities across Asia
Mongol conquest was destructive, but it also linked Afro-Eurasia
The Mongols invented the trade routes they controlled

why: Paragraph 1 says the memory of slaughter is deserved.
Paragraph 2 says trade routes became safer.

questions.stem: Which evidence does the historian use to support the claim that the Mongols "respected trade"?
options: Merchants dealt with one authority instead of many tolls
Hulegu sacked Baghdad and killed the caliph in 1258
Cities that resisted were destroyed so others would surrender
Mongol armies used terror as a weapon of war
questions.exp: One authority instead of a dozen rival rulers, plus repaired roads and punished bandits.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, which best describes a CHANGE in Silk Road trade under the Mongols?
options: Safer routes under one ruler carried more trade and ideas
Trade switched from overland routes to the sea because the roads were destroyed
Merchants stopped traveling because of Mongol violence
Religious differences closed the routes
questions.exp: The routes were old; Mongol unity made them safer and busier (the Pax Mongolica).
why: The passage says the roads were repaired.

questions.stem: The envoy's description of merchants in the quoted sentence best suggests that Calicut
options: was a dangerous port where merchants had to guard every cargo day and night
refused to let foreign merchants unload goods
had no market at all
was a safe, orderly market that trusted foreign traders
questions.exp: Merchants didn't bother with security or accounts: trade was safe and orderly.
why: He says they did not need to keep watch.
Goods went straight into the markets.

questions.stem: The third paragraph can best be used as evidence of which feature of Indian Ocean states?
options: Rulers built large navies to conquer the ports of their rivals across the ocean
Rulers banned foreign merchants
Rulers grew rich from duties on trade
Rulers depended on farming taxes alone
questions.exp: Customs duties gave states revenue from trade (compare Gujarat and Malacca).
why: The ruler sends out no ships of his own.
The passage stresses duties on goods.

questions.stem: The settling and marriage of Arab merchants described in the second paragraph most directly contributed to
options: the spread of Buddhism from India to China along the overland Silk Roads
the spread of Islam through family ties
the end of trade between Arabia and India
the Mongol conquest of southern India
questions.exp: Merchant intermarriage spread Islam through families rather than conquest.
why: Not in the passage or your cards.

options: The Indian Ocean carried goods too heavy for land
Only the Silk Roads used any new technology to make long-distance trade easier
Only the Indian Ocean carried luxury goods
The Silk Roads depended on monsoon winds

options: All three networks traded exactly the same goods along their routes
All three relied on monsoon winds
Each network had transport suited to its terrain
All three used flying cash
questions.exp: Caravans for land, ships for sea, camels and saddles for desert.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the historian's claim in the first paragraph?
options: The plague spread along the same routes as trade
The plague began in Europe and spread east along the roads to Central Asia
The plague spread only by sea
The Mongols stopped the plague
questions.exp: Fleas on rats rode ships and caravans; Mongol conquests helped carry it west.
why: It reached Europe from the east.

questions.stem: The second paragraph can best be used as evidence that the plague
options: strengthened landowners by giving them more power over the surviving peasants
lowered wages across Europe
had no effect on the countryside
weakened feudalism by making labor scarce
questions.exp: Labor shortages raised wages and weakened feudal obligations.

B1.title: A scholar on the Niger, c. 1352
B1.attr: Practice passage built around the words of Ibn Battuta, a Muslim scholar from Morocco. Only the words in quotation marks are his; they are quoted in your textbook.
B1.label: Practice passage written from your class materials; the quoted words are a real quotation from your textbook.
paras: Ibn Battuta began traveling at 21 and spent about thirty years visiting mostly Muslim lands, from Mali to China. Late in his travels he crossed the Sahara to Mali, then the richest kingdom in West Africa. He wrote as a Muslim scholar, and he paid close attention to how well the people he met followed the faith.

Of his trip along the river he wrote: "From Timbuktu I sailed down the Nile [Niger] on a small boat, hollowed out of a single piece of wood... I went on . . . to Gawgaw [Gao], which is a large city on the Nile [Niger]... The buying and selling of its inhabitants is done with cowry-shells, and the same is the case at Malli [the city of Mali]."

From Gao he joined "a large caravan of merchants from Ghadamas" heading north across the desert. Such caravans, with guides, provisions and thousands of camels, moved from oasis to oasis carrying the gold of West Africa north and returning with salt.

B2.title: Old tools, bigger scale
B2.attr: Practice passage written in the style of a modern economic historian.
B2.label: Practice passage written from your class materials (textbook, review sheet, slides); not a real quotation.
paras: Historians sometimes credit the Mongols with inventing the commercial tools of the Silk Roads, but the tools were older. Caravanserai, roadside inns where travelers could rest, store goods and stable their animals, had stood along the routes for centuries. China had long had a money economy, and its government had developed paper money and flying cash, a form of credit that let a merchant deposit money in one city and collect the same amount in another, because copper coins were too heavy to carry for large trades.

What changed after 1200 was scale. Under a single Mongol authority, these tools served many more merchants over far greater distances. In Europe, merchants used bills of exchange, promises to pay a set amount on a set date, and banking houses that handled such bills appeared in the 1300s.
The lesson is one of continuity as much as change: the age of the Mongols improved and spread the tools of trade more than it invented them.

B3.title: Towns of the coast
B3.attr: Practice passage in the voice of a medieval geographer describing the East African coast.
B3.label: Practice passage written from your class materials (textbook, review sheet, slides); not a real quotation.
paras: The towns of this coast, among them Kilwa, Mombasa and Mogadishu, are governed by their own rulers and look out on the sea. Their merchants buy gold and ivory from the peoples of the interior and sell them to the ships that arrive with the monsoon from Arabia, Persia and India. In return they receive cotton cloth from India, and porcelain from China is common in the houses of the rich.

The people speak a language of the coast that mixes their own Bantu speech with many Arabic words; the name the Arabs give them means "people of the coast." Most of the leading men are Muslims, for the Arab and Persian merchants who settled here married the daughters of local families, and their children grew up in the faith.
Enslaved people from the interior are also sold here and carried to North Africa, to the lands of the Arabs and to India, where they labor in the cities, serve in households or fight as soldiers.

B4.title: Goods carried across the Sahara
B4.attr: Built from the table in your textbook (AMSCO) and your review cards.
B4.label: Table adapted from your class materials.
table: Gold, ivory, enslaved people, kola nuts
Salt, horses, books, copper and brass

B5.title: Crops on the move
B5.attr: Practice passage written in the style of a modern environmental historian.
B5.label: Practice passage written from your class materials (textbook, review sheet, slides); not a real quotation.
paras: The trade networks of 1200 to 1450 carried seeds as well as silk. The Chinese court received a quick-ripening rice from the rulers of Champa, in what is now central Vietnam, as tribute. Because it resisted both drought and flood, a farmer could harvest two crops a year from the same field, and as it spread across southern China the population grew.

Across the Indian Ocean, Indonesian seafarers brought bananas to Sub-Saharan Africa. The nutritious fruit let Bantu-speaking farmers settle in places where yams did not grow, and their numbers rose. Citrus fruits moved through Muslim lands and markets such as Samarkand into the Mediterranean.

Yet more people meant more pressure on the land. Overgrazing, deforestation and soil erosion cut farm output in several regions; near Great Zimbabwe, overgrazing helped force people to abandon the city in the late 1400s.

questions.stem: The first paragraph suggests that a historian using Ibn Battuta's account should keep in mind that he
options: was a European merchant interested mainly in prices and the goods for sale
never actually visited West Africa
wrote as a Christian pilgrim
judged what he saw from a Muslim scholar's point of view
questions.exp: He wrote as a Muslim scholar who paid attention to how people followed the faith.

had no trade at all
used cowrie shells as currency
traded only by sea
questions.exp: "The buying and selling of its inhabitants is done with cowry-shells."

questions.stem: The caravans described in the third paragraph were made possible most directly by
options: camels and saddles suited to desert travel
the monsoon winds, which carried the caravans quickly across the open sand
the Mongol yam relay system
Chinese junks
questions.exp: Camels, which go long without water, and load-bearing saddles made the crossing practical.

questions.stem: Which best states the historian's argument?
options: The Mongols invented caravanserai, credit and paper money after they united Asia
Trade declined after 1200
The tools of trade were improved and spread, not invented
Europe invented all commercial tools
questions.exp: "Improved and spread the tools of trade more than it invented them."
why: The historian says the tools were older.
The passage credits China and Persia too.

questions.stem: According to the first paragraph, China developed flying cash because
options: the Mongols banned the use of coins and forced merchants to use paper instead
paper was cheaper than silk
banking houses required it
copper coins were too heavy for large trades
questions.exp: Deposit in one city, collect in another, because heavy coins were hard to carry.
why: The passage gives coin weight as the reason.

questions.stem: The European practice described in the second paragraph was most similar in purpose to
options: the caravanserai, where merchants could rest and stable animals on the roads
the camel saddle
China's flying cash
the lateen sail
questions.exp: Bills of exchange and flying cash both moved money without carrying coins.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the main idea of the first paragraph?
options: Coastal towns traded African goods for Asian goods
Coastal towns made porcelain and cotton cloth to sell to Chinese merchants
Coastal towns were ruled by China
Coastal towns traded only with each other
questions.exp: Gold and ivory went out; Indian cloth and Chinese porcelain came in.
why: Porcelain came from China and cloth from India.

questions.stem: The second paragraph can best be used as evidence of
options: the forced conversion of the coast by Arab armies after a long period of war
the isolation of the coast from Arabia
the spread of Buddhism in Africa
cultural blending caused by trade
questions.exp: A blended Bantu-Arabic language and Islam spreading through marriage.
why: Islam spread through marriage, not conquest.

questions.stem: The slave trade described in the third paragraph differed from the later Atlantic slave trade because enslaved people were
options: often used in cities, households and armies
sent mainly to work on large sugar plantations in the Americas for European owners
never sold to other regions
all from Asia
questions.exp: They labored in cities, served in households or fought as soldiers.
why: They came from the African interior.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the table?
options: West Africa produced all of its own salt, so salt was sent north to buyers there
Each region traded goods the other lacked
Horses moved south to north
Gold moved north to south
questions.exp: Gold from the south, salt from the north: each side supplied what the other lacked.

questions.stem: The flow of gold shown in the table most directly helped cause
options: the decline of West African kingdoms, which lost all of their gold to the north
the wealth of empires such as Mali
the spread of Buddhism in North Africa
the Mongol conquest of the Sahara
questions.exp: Mali taxed and protected the gold trade and grew richer than Ghana.
why: Mali grew rich by taxing the gold trade.

questions.stem: The first two paragraphs support which claim?
options: New crops reduced population because they replaced the older and healthier foods
New crops carried by trade led to population growth
Crops moved only by conquest
Crops never left their homelands
questions.exp: Champa rice and bananas fed growing populations.

questions.stem: The final paragraph shows which consequence of the developments described earlier?
options: Larger populations strained the land
Larger populations led to more forests, since farmers planted trees for fruit
Farm output rose without limit
Cities grew everywhere
questions.exp: Overgrazing, deforestation and soil erosion followed population growth.

sections.name: MCQ Set C
tips: Read the question stem before the source so you know what you are looking for.

For "best used as evidence of" or "best illustrates" questions, first name the idea the source shows (cause, effect, continuity, change, connection between regions), then pick the option that matches that idea.
Eliminate options that are true in history but not shown by the source, or that belong to the wrong time or region.
Watch for extreme words ("only," "all," "first," "created," "ended," "every"): they are usually wrong.
For "claim" or "evidence the author uses" questions, the answer must be stated or directly supported in the text. Do not use outside knowledge to pick it.
For point-of-view questions, ask who wrote it, when, for whom, and why.

S16.title: Angkor Thom
S16.attr: Adapted from a textbook description of the royal monuments of the Khmer Empire.
S16.label: Practice source (adapted for practice; not a verbatim quotation).
S16.text: The Khmer Empire, in present-day Cambodia, was the most successful kingdom in Southeast Asia. The royal monuments at Angkor Thom show both Hindu and Buddhist influences. Hindu artwork and sculptures of Hindu gods adorned the city. Later, when Khmer rulers had become Buddhist, they added Buddhist sculptures and artwork onto buildings while keeping the Hindu artwork.

S17.title: Cultural influences of Islam in Afro-Eurasia
S17.label: Practice source (adapted for practice).
table: The Swahili language blends Bantu and Arabic; Timbuktu became a center of Islamic learning; leaders deepened Islamic ties through pilgrimages to Mecca
Islam's emphasis on equality attracted lower-caste Hindus; architecture blended Hindu designs with Islamic patterns; the Urdu language drew on Hindi, Arabic, and Persian
Javanese stories, puppetry, and poetry absorbed Muslim characters and techniques

S18.title: Women in the Mongol Empire
S18.label: Practice source (adapted for practice; not a verbatim quotation).
S18.text: In the Mongols' nomadic culture, women tended flocks of sheep and goats in addition to raising children and providing meals. Because they rode horses as men did, Mongol women wore the same kind of leather trousers. They could remarry after being widowed and could start divorces. In the lands the Mongols ruled, Mongol women moved about freely, and women were often top advisors to the great khan.

S19.title: The kingdom of Gujarat
S19.label: Practice source (adapted for practice; not a verbatim quotation).
S19.text: The western Indian kingdom of Gujarat became the go-between for trade between the East and West. Its rulers raised money through customs, which were taxes on imported goods, and through fees for the use of seaports. The revenue from customs in Gujarat was many times greater than the entire worth of some European states.

S20.title: Learning and technology on the trade routes
S20.attr: Adapted summary of a textbook account.
S20.label: Practice source (written for practice; not a verbatim quotation).
paras: Islamic scholars translated Greek literary classics into Arabic, saving the works of Aristotle and other thinkers. They also brought back mathematics texts from India and techniques for making paper from China.
Papermaking reached Europe from China in the 13th century. Together with printing technology, it helped lead to a rise in literacy.

questions.stem: The monuments described in the passage best illustrate which of the following about the spread of Indian religions into Southeast Asia?
options: Buddhism completely replaced Hinduism once Khmer rulers converted.
Indian religions spread mainly when Indian armies conquered Southeast Asia.
Southeast Asian rulers rejected Indian religious influence in their architecture.
New religions were often added to earlier traditions rather than replacing them.
questions.exp: The Khmer rulers added Buddhist art while keeping the Hindu art, which shows that religions often blended or coexisted rather than replacing one another. Indian religions spread through trade, not conquest by Indian armies, and the monuments show acceptance of Indian influence, not rejection.
why: The monuments show Buddhist art added alongside Hindu art, not one replacing the other.
Indian religions spread through trade and contact, not conquest by Indian armies.
The Khmer rulers built Indian-influenced monuments, so they accepted rather than rejected Indian influence.

questions.stem: Which additional evidence would best support the claim that Khmer rulers used religion to strengthen their authority?
options: Merchants from India described the temples in letters sent home.
Sculptures showed kings sharing the powers of Hindu gods.
Farmers paid taxes in rice to support the builders of the city.
Buddhist monks lived in monasteries on the edges of the capital.
questions.exp: Showing kings as sharing divine powers directly links religion to royal authority, as in Khmer ideas of divine kingship. Travelers' letters, tax payments, and monks living nearby do not show religion being used to support rule.
why: Merchants' letters about the temples do not show rulers using religion to support their authority.
Farmers paying taxes in rice supports the builders but does not link religion to royal authority.
Monks living near the capital does not show rulers using religion to strengthen their rule.

questions.skill: Drawing an inference from a source
questions.stem: Which of the following can best be inferred about the role of religious imagery on the royal monuments?
options: It helped rulers collect customs duties from foreign merchants.
It showed that rulers wished to end earlier religious traditions.
Royal monuments linked the ruling family with divine imagery.
It was designed mainly to attract Chinese merchants to Cambodia.
questions.exp: Monuments built by rulers and filled with religious art tied the royal family to sacred authority; Khmer kings drew on Hindu ideas of divine kingship. Nothing in the passage connects the imagery to customs duties, ending older traditions, or attracting Chinese merchants.
why: Nothing links the religious imagery to customs duties.
The monuments kept older traditions alongside new ones, so rulers did not want to end them.
Attracting Chinese merchants is not mentioned as the purpose of the imagery.

questions.skill: Drawing a conclusion from a source
questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported by the information in the table?
options: The spread of Islam produced blended cultures rather than uniform ones.
Islam spread primarily through military conquest in each of the three regions listed.
Islamic learning remained limited to cities in sub-Saharan Africa.
Local traditions disappeared once Islam arrived in each region.
questions.exp: The Swahili language, blended architecture, Urdu, and Javanese puppetry with Muslim characters all show cultural blending. The table does not mention conquest, does not limit Islamic learning to Africa, and does not say local traditions disappeared.
why: The table does not say Islam spread mainly through conquest in all three regions.
The table does not say Islamic learning was limited to cities in sub-Saharan Africa.
The table shows local traditions blending with Islam, not disappearing.

questions.stem: A student claims Islam spread in South Asia mainly through force. Which detail in the table most directly challenges that claim?
options: Architecture blended Hindu designs with Islamic patterns.
Leaders in Africa deepened Islamic ties through pilgrimages to Mecca.
The Urdu language drew on Hindi, Arabic, and Persian.
Islam's emphasis on equality attracted lower-caste Hindus.
questions.exp: Lower-caste Hindus being attracted by Islam's emphasis on equality points to voluntary conversion for social reasons, which challenges the claim of force. The architecture and Urdu show blending, and the pilgrimage detail concerns Africa, not South Asia.
why: Blended architecture shows cultural mixing but does not address whether conversion was forced.
The pilgrimage detail concerns Africa, not South Asia.
Urdu shows blending but says nothing about whether Islam spread by force.

questions.stem: The existence of the Urdu language best illustrates
options: the replacement of Persian by Arabic across South Asia.
Mongol efforts to unify their empire under one script.
cultural blending that followed Islam's arrival in South Asia.
the isolation of South Asian languages from outside influence.
questions.exp: Urdu drew on Hindi, Arabic, and Persian, which shows blending after Islam arrived. Uyghur script, not Urdu, was the Mongol writing system, and Urdu neither replaced Persian nor shows isolation.
why: Urdu drew on Persian as well as Arabic; it did not show Persian being replaced.
The Mongol script was Uyghur, not Urdu.
Urdu drew on Hindi, Arabic, and Persian, so it shows outside influence, not isolation.

questions.stem: The passage best illustrates which of the following about gender in Afro-Eurasia in this period?
options: Women gained equal political power in nearly every society of the period.
Women's roles varied, and some enjoyed more freedom than was typical.
Nomadic societies gave women fewer rights than farming societies did.
Patriarchal norms vanished in every society the Mongols conquered.
questions.exp: Mongol women had more freedom than women in most other parts of Afro-Eurasia, even though the empire was still a patriarchy. The passage does not support equal power everywhere, fewer rights for nomadic women, or the disappearance of patriarchy.
why: 'Equal political power in nearly every society' is much stronger than the passage supports.
The passage says Mongol women had more freedom, not fewer rights.
The empire was still a patriarchy; norms did not vanish.

questions.stem: The roles of Mongol women are best used to illustrate which of the following about the relationship between environment and society?
options: A way of life shaped by environment could produce different gender roles.
Religious teachings were the main source of gender norms in every society.
Wealth from conquest was the main reason women gained greater freedom.
Patriarchal norms were weaker wherever long-distance trade was heavy.
questions.exp: Herding and horse-riding on the steppe gave women practical roles that differed from those in settled societies, which shows how environment and way of life shaped gender roles. The other options rely on extreme or unsupported claims such as 'in every society' and 'wherever trade was heavy.'
why: 'Main source in every society' is an extreme claim the passage does not make.
Wealth from conquest is not given as the reason women had freedom.
'Wherever long-distance trade was heavy' is unsupported by the passage.

questions.stem: The freedoms of Mongol women are best used as evidence of which of the following?
options: Social structures were identical in every single part of the Mongol Empire.
Mongol rule ended class distinctions among the people it conquered.
The Mongol Empire was the only patriarchal society in Afro-Eurasia.
Gender norms differed even among societies that were mostly patriarchal.
questions.exp: Societies were mostly patriarchal, yet Mongol women had more freedom than most, which shows variation. The other options rely on extreme words: "identical," "ended," and "only."
why: 'Identical in every single part' is far too extreme.
The passage does not say Mongol rule ended class distinctions.
'The only patriarchal society' is false; most societies were patriarchal.

questions.stem: The information in the passage can best be used as evidence that
options: Indian Ocean states relied mainly on farming to pay for their governments.
states could grow wealthy by taxing trade that passed through their ports.

sections.name: SAQs
tips: Use TEA for every part: T = Topic sentence (answer the question directly, restating its words), E = Evidence (a specific person, place, term, date, or detail from the source or your knowledge), A = Analysis (explain how that evidence proves your topic sentence, using "which led to," "because," or "this allowed").
Label your answers A, B, and C and write in complete sentences. No introduction or thesis.
Each part is worth 1 point. Name a specific, accurate piece of evidence (a person, place, term, date, or technology), then explain how it connects to what the question asks.
"Describe" means give accurate details. "Explain" means show how or why, using a link such as "which led to," "because," or "this allowed."
Stay inside 1200 to 1450 unless the question says otherwise.
Sentence frame: "One way ___ was ___. For example, ___. This mattered because ___."
Aim for about 13 minutes per SAQ on the real test: about 1 to plan and 12 to write.

Self-check before you reveal the answer: Did I give a specific example, not just a general idea? Did I explain the connection? Is it the right time and place? Did I answer the exact verb (describe or explain)?

parts.prompt: Describe one claim Matthew Paris makes about the Mongols.
parts.skill: Describing a claim from a source
parts.model: One claim Matthew Paris makes is that the Mongols caused terrible destruction in eastern Europe. He writes that they "razed cities, cut down forests, overthrown fortresses" and "killed townspeople and peasants." This shows he portrays the Mongols as a destructive invading force that attacked civilians as well as armies.
tea: One claim Matthew Paris makes is that the Mongols caused terrible destruction in eastern Europe.
He writes that they "razed cities, cut down forests, overthrown fortresses" and "killed townspeople and peasants."
This shows he portrays the Mongols as a destructive invading force that attacked civilians as well as armies.
parts.earns: You accurately describe any specific claim in the passage (for example, that the Mongols razed cities, killed civilians, destroyed farmland, or passed through Muslim lands before reaching Europe).
parts.weak: "He says the Mongols were bad." This does not name a specific claim from the text.

parts.prompt: Explain one way that Mongol rule, despite the violence described in the excerpt, helped expand networks of exchange between 1200 and 1450.
parts.skill: Explaining a cause with specific evidence
parts.model: One way Mongol rule expanded networks of exchange was by making Silk Roads travel safer, a period known as the Pax Mongolica. The Mongols improved roads, punished bandits, and ran the yam, a relay system of posts with fresh horses and supplies. With less risk of robbery and faster, safer travel, merchants could carry goods farther across Eurasia, which increased trade between East Asia, the Middle East, and Europe.

The Mongols improved roads, punished bandits, and ran the yam, a relay system of posts with fresh horses and supplies.
With less risk of robbery and faster, safer travel, merchants could carry goods farther across Eurasia, which increased trade between East Asia, the Middle East, and Europe.
parts.earns: You name a specific Mongol policy or condition (Pax Mongolica, safer roads, punished banditry, the yam relay, one authority that respected merchants, religious tolerance) and explain how it increased trade.
parts.weak: "The Mongols helped trade a lot." (No specific evidence and no explanation.) Also avoid saying the Mongols created the Silk Roads; the routes already existed.

parts.prompt: Explain one cultural, technological, or environmental effect of the increased connections that Mongol rule created.

parts.model: One effect of the connections Mongol rule created was the spread of the bubonic plague. The Black Death traveled along trade routes from Central Asia and reached Europe by 1347, killing roughly a third of Europe's people. Because Mongol-linked routes moved people and goods quickly over huge distances, they also moved disease, and the resulting labor shortages in Europe raised wages.
tea: One effect of the connections Mongol rule created was the spread of the bubonic plague.
The Black Death traveled along trade routes from Central Asia and reached Europe by 1347, killing roughly a third of Europe's people.
Because Mongol-linked routes moved people and goods quickly over huge distances, they also moved disease, and the resulting labor shortages in Europe raised wages.
parts.earns: You give one specific effect (a technology, body of knowledge, religion, crop, or disease) and explain how the connections caused it.
parts.weak: "Ideas and diseases spread." This names no specific example and does not explain the link.

Paper money, silk made in large amounts for sale, and imports from other provinces show goods were bought and sold across a large market, not just made for local use.

parts.earns: You accurately describe any trade-related detail from the passage (paper money, large-scale silk production, or merchants importing goods).

parts.prompt: Explain one way that commercial innovations such as the one Polo mentions helped long-distance trade grow between 1200 and 1450.
parts.skill: Explaining a cause with specific evidence
parts.model: One way paper money helped long-distance trade grow was by making large payments easier to carry and trust. Chinese flying cash and paper money let a merchant deposit money in one city and withdraw it in another, and bills of exchange worked in a similar way. Merchants no longer had to haul heavy copper coins over dangerous routes, so they could make larger deals over longer distances, which increased trade along the Silk Roads.

Polo was a Venetian merchant who visited the court of Kublai Khan and wrote about China after returning to Italy in 1295. As an outsider focused on trade, he may have exaggerated or ignored parts of Chinese society that did not interest merchants, so historians must check his account against Chinese sources.

tips: Read the attribution line first: who wrote it, when, and why. A Ming official, a Muslim scholar and a modern historian each have a different purpose.
Find the main idea of each paragraph before you look at the choices. Many questions ask about one paragraph only.

For "best used as evidence of" or "best illustrates" questions, first name the bigger development the source shows (more trade, Mongol connections, spread of religion, crops and disease), then pick the choice that matches it.
The wrong choices are usually true-but-not-in-the-source, from the wrong network or region, or too extreme. Cross them out with the X button.

M1.title: Against the treasure fleets
M1.attr: Practice passage in the voice of a Confucian official at the Ming court, written after the death of the Yongle emperor.
M1.label: Practice passage written from your class materials (textbook, review sheet, slides); not a real quotation.
paras: The treasure fleets of the admiral Zheng He have sailed seven times, as far as the coasts of Arabia and Africa. Hundreds of ships went out at a time, and each voyage cost the treasury sums that could have fed whole provinces. The fleets were sent to show the might of the Ming and to bring back tribute, and they returned with rare animals and spices.

But these are curiosities that add nothing to the strength of the empire. The foundation of the empire is the farmer and the family, as the sages taught. Sailors who spend years among foreign peoples learn foreign customs and forget their duties to their ancestors and their ruler.
The new emperor would do well to end these voyages, keep the people at home and forbid subjects to sail abroad, so that the empire may rest on its own fields.

M2.title: The court of Kublai Khan
M2.attr: Practice passage written in the style of a modern historian of Yuan China.
M2.label: Practice passage written from your class materials (textbook, review sheet, slides); not a real quotation.
paras: Kublai Khan, grandson of Genghis, became Great Khan in 1260 and founded the Yuan dynasty in China in 1271. In many ways his rule was more Chinese than Mongol: he rebuilt the capital as Dadu and took on the style of a Chinese emperor. He allowed the peoples of his empire to follow their own religions and consulted Buddhist monks, Daoist priests, Muslim scholars and Christian missionaries at his court. Foreigners such as the Venetian merchant Marco Polo were welcomed.

Yet Kublai and his successors did not trust the Chinese elite. They gave high office to foreigners, set aside the civil service examinations that had long opened government to educated Chinese, and kept themselves apart from the people they ruled. The scholar-gentry, shut out of the positions they believed were theirs, came to resent Mongol rule.

As the Black Death and revolts weakened Mongol power in the 1300s, that resentment fed rebellion. Secret groups such as the White Lotus Society organized against the Yuan, and in 1368 a former monk from a poor peasant family, Zhu Yuanzhang, drove the Mongols out and founded the Ming.

M3.title: How Islam traveled
M3.attr: Practice passage written in the style of a modern historian of world religions.
M3.label: Practice passage written from your class materials (textbook, review sheet, slides); not a real quotation.
paras: Islam spread across much of Afro-Eurasia between 1200 and 1450, but the sword was only one of its paths. Along the trade routes, merchants carried the faith as they carried goods. In West Africa, rulers such as the kings of Mali adopted Islam, and Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 announced Mali's place in the Muslim world. Timbuktu became a center of Islamic learning. Yet most West Africans kept their traditional beliefs.

Around the Indian Ocean, Arab and Persian merchants settled in port cities, married local women and raised their children as Muslims. On the East African coast, this produced the Swahili culture and a language that blends Bantu and Arabic. In Southeast Asia, the rulers of Malacca, a city-state that grew rich from ships passing its strait, became Muslim.
In South Asia, contact between Muslims and Hindus produced new blends, such as the Urdu language, which joins Hindi with Arabic and Persian.

M5.title: Faiths that blended
M5.attr: Practice passage written in the style of a modern historian of Asia.
M5.label: Practice passage written from your class materials (textbook, review sheet, slides); not a real quotation.
paras: When religions traveled along the trade routes, they rarely replaced what was already there. More often they blended with it. Buddhism came from India to China along the Silk Roads, and the monk Xuanzang helped make it popular. In China it mixed with Daoist ideas to form Chan Buddhism, known in Japan as Zen, which became popular with ordinary people.

Neo-Confucianism blended the rational thought of Confucius with Daoist and Buddhist ideas, and it became the state ideology of Korea and spread to Japan and Vietnam. In Southeast Asia, the Khmer Empire's monuments at Angkor show both Hindu and Buddhist influences: later Buddhist rulers added their own sculptures to buildings while keeping the Hindu artwork.
Historians call this process syncretism: the blending of beliefs from different traditions into something new.

examTips: Turn the Timer on and give yourself about 13 minutes per SAQ (1 to plan and 12 to write).
Write complete sentences for A, B, and C, and only then click Check Answer.
tips: Use TEA for every part: T = Topic sentence (answer the question directly, restating its words), E = Evidence (a specific person, place, term, date, or detail from the source or your knowledge), A = Analysis (explain how that evidence proves your topic sentence, using "which led to," "because," or "this allowed").
Label your answers A, B, and C and write in complete sentences. No introduction or thesis.
Each part is worth 1 point. Name a specific, accurate piece of evidence (a person, place, term, date, or technology), then explain how it connects to what the question asks.
"Describe" means give accurate details. "Explain" means show how or why, using a link such as "which led to," "because," or "this allowed."
Stay inside 1200 to 1450 unless the question says otherwise.
Sentence frame: "One way ___ was ___. For example, ___. This mattered because ___."
Aim for about 13 minutes per SAQ on the real test: about 1 to plan and 12 to write.

Self-check before you reveal the answer: Did I give a specific example, not just a general idea? Did I explain the connection? Is it the right time and place? Did I answer the exact verb (describe or explain)?

MS1.title: The Sultanate of Malacca
MS1.attr: Adapted summary of a textbook account.
MS1.label: Practice source (written for practice; not a verbatim quotation).
MS1.text: The Sultanate of Malacca, a Muslim city-state on the Strait of Malacca, grew wealthy by charging fees on the ships that passed through the strait between India and China. Its sultans built a navy to keep the waters safe from pirates, and in the 1400s the state expanded into Sumatra and the southern Malay Peninsula. Merchants from Arabia, India, China, and Southeast Asia lived and traded in the city until the Portuguese conquered it in 1511.

parts.prompt: Describe one way Malacca's rulers used the city's location to gain wealth, according to the excerpt.
parts.skill: Describing a claim from a source
parts.model: Malacca's rulers used the city's location to gain wealth by charging fees on passing ships. The excerpt says the sultanate grew wealthy "by charging fees on the ships that passed through the strait between India and China." Because ships traveling between India and China had to pass through the strait, the fees created a steady stream of income.
tea: Malacca's rulers used the city's location to gain wealth by charging fees on passing ships.
The excerpt says the sultanate grew wealthy "by charging fees on the ships that passed through the strait between India and China."
Because ships traveling between India and China had to pass through the strait, the fees created a steady stream of income.
parts.earns: You accurately describe a way stated in the passage (fees on passing ships, or building a navy to keep the strait safe so trade would continue).
parts.weak: "They traded a lot." This does not describe how the location produced wealth.

parts.prompt: Explain one way that knowledge of the monsoon winds contributed to the growth of trading cities such as Malacca between 1200 and 1450.
parts.skill: Explaining a cause with specific evidence
parts.model: Knowledge of the monsoon winds helped trading cities grow by forcing merchants to stop and wait in port. Winter winds blew from the northeast and summer winds from the southwest, so merchants had to wait in cities such as Malacca for the winds to change. Waiting merchants bought, sold, and paid fees, so the city's population and wealth grew.
tea: Knowledge of the monsoon winds helped trading cities grow by forcing merchants to stop and wait in port.
Winter winds blew from the northeast and summer winds from the southwest, so merchants had to wait in cities such as Malacca for the winds to change.
Waiting merchants bought, sold, and paid fees, so the city's population and wealth grew.
parts.earns: You link monsoon timing to a specific consequence for trading cities (merchants waiting in port, ports becoming meeting points, more trade and wealth).
parts.weak: "The wind helped them sail." This does not explain how the winds helped cities grow.

parts.prompt: Explain one way diasporic merchant communities affected the cultures of Indian Ocean port cities.
parts.skill: Explaining an effect with specific evidence
parts.model: Diasporic merchant communities blended cultures in Indian Ocean port cities. Arab and Persian merchants settled in ports such as those on the Swahili coast and in western India, married local women, and introduced Islam and the Arabic language. Local cultures also influenced the merchants, producing blended cultures such as Swahili language and culture.
tea: Diasporic merchant communities blended cultures in Indian Ocean port cities.
Arab and Persian merchants settled in ports such as those on the Swahili coast and in western India, married local women, and introduced Islam and the Arabic language.
Local cultures also influenced the merchants, producing blended cultures such as Swahili language and culture.
parts.earns: You name a specific community or place and a specific cultural effect (the spread of Islam, a blended language, intermarriage, or two-way influence).
parts.weak: "Different people lived together." This names no specific community or effect.

Growth is linked to political stability and strong farm output, while decline is linked to instability, invasions, and falling agricultural productivity. This shows a city's fortunes depended on political security and its food supply as well as on trade.

Growth is linked to political stability and strong farm output, while decline is linked to instability, invasions, and falling agricultural productivity.
This shows a city's fortunes depended on political security and its food supply as well as on trade.

parts.weak: "There are many factors." This is not a pattern from the table.

parts.prompt: Explain one way that trade networks contributed to the growth of a specific city between 1200 and 1450.
parts.skill: Explaining a cause with specific evidence
parts.model: Trade networks made Timbuktu grow. Mali's rulers taxed and protected the trans-Saharan gold trade, and Mansa Musa built mosques and schools there. The wealth and Islamic learning drew merchants and scholars, which made Timbuktu a major center of trade and learning. (Other strong answers: Samarkand, Kashgar, Hangzhou, Malacca.)
tea: Trade networks made Timbuktu grow.
Mali's rulers taxed and protected the trans-Saharan gold trade, and Mansa Musa built mosques and schools there.
The wealth and Islamic learning drew merchants and scholars, which made Timbuktu a major center of trade and learning. (Other strong answers: Samarkand, Kashgar, Hangzhou, Malacca.)
parts.earns: You name a specific city and explain how a trade network caused its growth.
parts.weak: "Trade made cities bigger." This names no city and gives no specific link.

parts.prompt: Explain one reason a specific trading city declined between 1200 and 1450.

parts.model: Baghdad declined because of foreign invasion. The Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258 and killed many of its residents. The destruction of the city and its people ended its role as a major political and trading center. (Other strong answers: Constantinople after 1204 and plague; Kashgar after Tamerlane's attacks.)
tea: Baghdad declined because of foreign invasion.
The Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258 and killed many of its residents.
The destruction of the city and its people ended its role as a major political and trading center. (Other strong answers: Constantinople after 1204 and plague; Kashgar after Tamerlane's attacks.)
parts.earns: You name a specific city and give a specific cause of its decline (invasion, plague, or political instability) with evidence.
parts.weak: "Cities declined because of problems." This names no city or cause.
